h1: Whisky auctions and the secondary market
title: Whisky Auctions and Resale | Craft Beer School
desc: How whisky auctions and the secondary market work: fees, fill levels, provenance, fakes and the legal limits on buying and selling from India.
teaser: The hammer price is not what you pay. Here is how whisky auctions really work.
standfirst: Whisky auctions let collectors find bottles that left the shops years ago. They also come with fees, fakes and legal limits that catch Indian buyers out. Here is how the market works before you place a bid.
sections:
Most whisky auctions now run online. A seller consigns bottles and may set a reserve, a minimum price below which the bottle will not sell. Buyers bid over a set period. The highest bid when the auction closes is the hammer price.

The hammer price is not the final cost. The auction house adds a buyer's premium, usually a percentage of the hammer price, plus tax on that premium where it applies. Shipping, insurance and any import duties come on top. Sellers pay their own commission and listing fees.

Read the terms for each auction house before you register. Fees, payment deadlines and what happens if a bottle arrives broken all differ.

Work it through with an example. Say a bottle hammers at ₹20,000 and the house charges a premium of 10% plus tax on the premium. You are already past ₹22,000 before shipping. Add insurance, packing and any customs duty and the real cost can be far above the number you bid.

Do that sum before you bid, not after. Set your maximum as the total cost you are willing to pay, then work back to the highest hammer price that fits.
Whisky does not age in the bottle

A whisky's age is the time it spent in the cask. Once bottled, it stops changing in any meaningful way. A twelve year old whisky bottled in 1990 is still a twelve year old whisky today. Our guide to whisky age statements explains what the number means.

So an old bottle is valuable for rarity, history or a distillery that has closed, not because the whisky has improved. Collectors pay for scarcity. Drinkers should remember that the liquid inside is the same as on the day it was bottled.

Look closely at the fill level. Whisky can slowly evaporate through a cork over decades, leaving a gap below the neck. Low fill can mean oxidation or a poor seal. Check the condition of the cork, the capsule, the label and the box. Auction listings should show clear photos of each.

Storage history matters too. A bottle kept upright in a cool, dark cupboard has had a far easier life than one that sat on a sunny shelf. Ask the auction house if the listing does not say.

Labels and boxes matter more to collectors than to drinkers. A torn label can halve the interest in a bottle without changing the whisky at all. Decide which you are before you bid.

Most major whisky auctions are based abroad. Many do not ship to India at all. Couriers often refuse alcohol. Bringing whisky in for personal use attracts customs duty. The state you live in may also limit how much you can possess.

Rules change with budgets and state policies. Check the current customs position on the CBIC website and your state's excise rules before you bid. Winning a bottle you cannot legally bring home is an expensive lesson.
Selling in India is harder still

In India, selling liquor generally needs a licence from the state excise department. Reselling a bottle from your collection, even privately, can fall foul of those rules. The details vary by state and change, so check before you sell anything. This is not legal advice.

That makes whisky a poor investment plan for most Indian collectors. Collect bottles you want to drink or share, not bottles you hope to flip. Our guide to starting a whisky collection in India covers a sensible approach.

The higher a bottle's price, the more attractive it is to counterfeiters. Rare old bottles are the most faked, because few people have tasted the real thing to compare. Reputable auction houses check provenance, but no system is perfect.

Ask where a bottle came from and how it was stored. Be wary of a rare bottle at a low price. Our guide to spotting counterfeit whisky covers the warning signs.

Pick one whisky you are curious about. Follow it across a few auctions without bidding. Note each hammer price in a simple spreadsheet, with the date, the fill level and the condition notes.

After a few months, you will know what that bottle really sells for and what drives the price up or down. Then you can bid with numbers rather than hope. If you never bid at all, you will still have learned how the market values age, condition and rarity, which is useful knowledge for any collector.
faqs: What is a buyer's premium at a whisky auction?
A fee the auction house adds to the hammer price, usually a percentage, often with tax on top. Shipping and duty are extra.
Does whisky get better with age in the bottle?
No. Whisky stops ageing once it is bottled. An old bottle is valued for rarity, not because the whisky improved.
Can I buy whisky at auction and ship it to India?
Often not. Many auction houses do not ship to India, couriers refuse alcohol and customs duty applies. Check customs and state rules before bidding.
